report.summary: LLM-as-judge reliability for code: In general LLM evaluation, Zheng et al. (2024, 'Judging LLM-as-a-Judge') report GPT-4 agreement with human pairwise preferences at ~85% on MT-Bench, but lower for more nuanced tasks. For code, studies like Li et al. (2024, 'Can LLMs Be Good Reviewers?') find LLM agreement with human reviewers around 60-70% (uncertain exact figure). Position bias: LLMs prefer first response ~10-20% more often (Zheng et al.). Verbosity bias: longer responses are rated higher; controlled tests show adjusting for length reduces reliability. Ensembling: using multiple LLMs and maj
risks: Over-reliance on LLM judges for code correctness without test verification may introduce subtle bugs.
Position and verbosity biases can skew results if not controlled.
Ensemble approaches increase cost and latency.
todos: Implement position randomization and length normalization in judge prompts.
Design detailed rubrics for code quality dimensions (correctness, readability, efficiency).
Set up an ensemble of at least three different LLM judges with majority voting.
Pilot the judge protocol on a sample set with human annotations to measure agreement and calibrate biases.

handoff.suggestion: Implement rubric-based evaluation with position randomization and ensemble of LLM judges (e.g., GPT-4, Claude, Llama 3) for code reviews. Validate on your internal dataset by computing Cohen's kappa with human raters on a subset of 200 samples to establish baseline agreement and bias effects before full deployment.
